item.title: System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning (NeurIPS 2025) [1], Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, and Sung Ju Hwang (KAIST, DeepAuto.ai) introduce MetaSPO, a bilevel optimization framework that meta-learns a task-agnostic system prompt while simultaneously updating task-specific user prompts in an iterative inner loop.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities, with optimizing their input prompts playing a pivotal role in maximizing their performance. However, while LLM prompts consist of both the task-agnostic system prompts and task-specific user prompts, existing work on prompt optimization has focused on user prompts specific to individual queries or tasks, and largely overlooked the system prompt that is, once optimized, applicable across different tasks and domains. Motivated by this, we introduce the novel problem of bilevel system prompt optimization, whose objective is to design system prompts that are robust to diverse user prompts and transferable to unseen tasks. To tackle this problem, we then propose a meta-learning framework, which meta-learns the system prompt by optimizing it over various user prompts across multiple datasets, while simultaneously updating the user prompts in an iterative manner to ensure synergy between them. We conduct experiments on 14 unseen datasets spanning 5 different domains, on which we show that our approach produces system prompts that generalize effectively to diverse user prompts. Also, our findings reveal that the optimized system prompt enables rapid adaptation even to unseen tasks, requiring fewer optimization steps for test-time user prompts while achieving improved performance.

Methods

Against this three-part structure, MetaSPO’s bilevel algorithm runs two nested optimization loops. The outer loop optimizes the task-agnostic system prompt, and the inner loop iteratively refines task-specific user prompts. At each outer step, the current system prompt is paired with candidate user prompts across multiple source tasks. The model’s failures on held-out examples feed an LLM optimizer that proposes refined candidates (user prompts inside the inner loop, system prompts at the outer loop). The meta-learned system prompt transfers to unseen target tasks with no further system-prompt tuning; at test time, only the user prompt is adapted per target task.

The system prompt starts as “You are a helpful assistant.” (the Default baseline) and is iteratively refined through the outer loop. At each step of either loop, a separate optimizer LLM (GPT-4o mini in the main experiments, distinct from the Llama-3.2 3B base LLM that generates task responses) is prompted with the current prompt and its incorrectly-predicted examples, asked to analyze the failure modes, and then asked for multiple candidate refinements. Candidates are evaluated against held-out task data, and the top-k by performance survive to the next iteration. Both loops follow this same textual-gradient pattern (after Pryzant et al. [4]), applied at different scopes: user prompt per task in the inner loop, system prompt aggregated across source tasks in the outer loop.

Results

The paper evaluates on 14 unseen target tasks across 5 domains (Medical, Review Analysis, Reasoning, Safety, Grounding), with each score the average performance of a system prompt paired with ten different user prompts. Within-domain Domain MetaSPO averages 44.5 over the 14 tasks, beating the next-best baseline SPRIG at 37.0 and the no-system-prompt Default at 32.2. The cross-domain Global MetaSPO setting (one system prompt meta-learned across all 5 domains) averages 41.4, still ahead of all baselines but ~3 points behind the within-domain Domain setting. Separately, on test-time efficiency: a MetaSPO-pretrained system prompt reaches Default’s converged performance with 80% fewer optimization iterations and 75% less data during test-time user-prompt adaptation.

Figure 4 tests whether MetaSPO’s lift transfers uniformly across target tasks or depends on source-target task similarity. The paper measures similarity via Bag-of-Words overlap between the source-task training distribution and the target task, then plots per-task improvement against it.

My Notes

  • The decomposition is the contribution, more than the method. Before this paper, “prompt optimization” treated the prompt as one optimization target for one task. DSPy [2], MIPRO [3], Pryzant et al.’s textual gradients [4], and EvoPrompt [5] each target a different piece of that setup, but all produce task-specific prompts. The bilevel split (task-agnostic system prompt above, task-specific user prompt below) is the key move; once you make it, the meta-learning structure follows naturally because the outer loop has a natural “across tasks” loss to optimize. The MetaSPO algorithm itself is a structurally familiar inner/outer LLM-as-optimizer loop. What matters here is the decision about what to put in each level.
  • The system prompt does most of the transfer work.
    • MetaSPO’s headline wins on unseen tasks come from the system prompt. In Table 1’s Unseen Generalization scenario, user prompts are LLM-sampled per task and held fixed; only the system prompt varies across the methods compared. Domain MetaSPO averages 44.5 over 14 unseen target tasks vs. Default’s 32.2, a +12.3-point lift attributable to the system prompt alone.
    • Appendix B.7 tests system-prompt vs user-prompt optimization head-to-head: MetaSPO (system-prompt optimized on source tasks) vs. ProTeGi (user-prompt optimized on source tasks), evaluated on the unseen Reasoning domain. MetaSPO wins across every source-domain starting point; ProTeGi drops below the Default system prompt, indicating user-prompt optimizations don’t transfer past the specific tasks they were tuned on.
  • Test-time efficiency is the practically relevant finding. The headline number is the unseen-generalization performance, but the deployment-relevant result is in §4: a MetaSPO-pretrained system prompt reaches the Default baseline’s converged performance with 80% fewer optimization iterations and 75% less data during test-time user-prompt adaptation. That’s a recipe for shipping prompt-optimized agents when each new task gets a small calibration budget rather than full re-optimization.
  • Generalization is asymmetric along source-target similarity. Figure 4 shows MetaSPO’s gain over Default scales with source-target task similarity measured by Bag-of-Words. High similarity, big gain; low similarity, the meta-learned system prompt is closer to neutral. That’s the expected meta-learning failure mode on out-of-distribution tasks, but it also bounds the deployment story: a system prompt meta-learned on Medical+Review+Reasoning will help most on tasks that look like those at the BoW level, and the cross-domain Global setting underperforms the within-domain Domain setting (41.4 vs. 44.5 avg). The follow-up question: at what point does the meta-learned prior become a liability on a sufficiently distant task?

  3. Opsahl-Ong, K., Ryan, M.   4. Pryzant, R., Iter, D., Li, J., Lee, Y., Zhu, C., Zeng, M. “Automatic Prompt Optimization with ‘Gradient Descent’ and Beam Search.” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.03495
  5. Guo, Q., Wang, R., Guo, J., Li, B., Song, K., Tan, X., Liu, G., Bian, J., Yang, Y. “EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024. arXiv:2309.08532. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08532

Related Posts

  • DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines: the prior-art prompt-optimization substrate MetaSPO cites, which it extends by splitting the prompt into a transferable system level and a task-specific user level.
  • EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers: an earlier LLM-as-optimizer loop that, like every method before MetaSPO, produces task-specific prompts rather than a task-agnostic one.
  • Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies: the same staging-is-the-contribution pattern, adding a search wrapper around an off-the-shelf prompt optimizer instead of a bilevel meta-learning loop.
  • GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning: a textual-gradient prompt optimizer in the same lineage as the Pryzant-style inner loop MetaSPO builds on.
  • Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: the position paper that classifies MetaSPO’s hand-fixed search structure as extrinsic, with humans choosing what each level optimizes.

item.title: ReMA: Learning to Meta-think for LLMs with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In ReMA: Learning to Meta-think for LLMs with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning [1], Ziyu Wan, Yunxiang Li, Ying Wen, and eight co-authors from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai AI Laboratory, UBC, and UCL train two large language model (LLM) agents jointly — a high-level meta-thinking agent that plans, and a low-level reasoning agent that executes — and show the split beats R1-style single-agent reinforcement learning on math and LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks.

Recent research on Reasoning of Large Language Models (LLMs) has sought to further enhance their performance by integrating meta-thinking — enabling models to monitor, evaluate, and control their reasoning processes for more adaptive and effective problem-solving. However, current single-agent work lacks a specialized design for acquiring meta-thinking, resulting in low efficacy. To address this challenge, we introduce Reinforced Meta-thinking Agents (ReMA), a novel framework that leverages Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to elicit meta-thinking behaviors, encouraging LLMs to think about thinking. ReMA decouples the reasoning process into two hierarchical agents: a high-level meta-thinking agent responsible for generating strategic oversight and plans, and a low-level reasoning agent for detailed executions. Through iterative reinforcement learning with aligned objectives, these agents explore and learn collaboration, leading to improved generalization and robustness. Empirical results from single-turn experiments demonstrate that ReMA outperforms single-agent RL baselines on complex reasoning tasks, including competitive-level mathematical benchmarks and LLM-as-a-Judge benchmarks. Additionally, we further extend ReMA to multi-turn interaction settings, leveraging turn-level ratio and parameter sharing to improve efficiency. Comprehensive ablation studies further illustrate the evolving dynamics of each distinct agent, providing valuable insights into how the meta-thinking reasoning process enhances the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

Preliminaries

The paper builds on a few standard objects:

  • Vanilla Reasoning Process (VRP) — autoregressive decoding from question to a reasoning trajectory from which the final answer is extracted: . This is the chain-of-thought (CoT) [2] baseline.
  • Meta-thinking Reasoning Process (MRP) — a single-agent variant that first emits a meta-thought , then conditions reasoning on it: . “Meta-thinking” means the model’s ability to monitor, evaluate, and control its own reasoning.
  • RL objective — both VRP and MRP optimize , where the verifiable reward compares the generated answer to the gold answer .
  • GRPO — Group Relative Policy Optimization [3], a PPO [4] variant that drops the learned critic. For each prompt, rollouts produce rewards ; the group-normalized advantage replaces the value baseline, and the clipped surrogate is applied per token, with .

ReMA replaces the single policy in MRP with two separately parameterized agents and casts joint training as multi-agent RL.

Non-conventional notation used in the rest of the post:

  • — meta-thinking output (a strategic plan or decomposition of ); — gold answer.
  • — parameters of the high-level (meta-thinking) and low-level (reasoning) agents.
  • — rewards used to update the high-level and low-level agents.
  • — group size, the number of rollouts sampled per prompt for advantage normalization.
  • Indices: ranges over rollouts in a group, over tokens within a rollout, over turns in a multi-turn rollout.
  • — group-normalized advantage for token of rollout .
  • vs — token-level importance ratio (GRPO) vs turn-averaged ratio (MAMRP).

Methods

The cover figure positions ReMA against two prior families:

  • Construction-based methods (left) fine-tune LLMs on rejection-sampled combinations of pre-defined templates — meta-thinking is hardcoded into the data, not learned.
  • R1-style methods (middle) train a single powerful LLM with reinforcement learning to interleave meta-thinking and detailed reasoning inside one generation.
  • ReMA (right) splits the two roles into separately parameterized agents — a high-level meta-thinker and a low-level reasoner — and updates both jointly with multi-agent reinforcement learning.

R1-style here is shorthand for DeepSeek R1 [5]: a single LLM trained with pure RL on verifiable rewards, which learns to produce long traces that mix strategic reflection with step-by-step reasoning in one generation.

The single-turn formulation factorizes generation into two sequential agent calls:

  • High-level agent takes the question and emits meta-thinking — a strategic plan or decomposition.
  • Low-level agent takes and emits the detailed reasoning trajectory .
  • The joint policy factorizes as .

Each agent is trained iteratively under its own reward, conditioned on the other’s policy:

Training alternates between freezing one agent and updating the other with PPO/GRPO, so each policy improves while its partner is held fixed.

The training-pipeline figure makes the architectural difference concrete:

  • Left is single-agent RL — VRP mixes meta-thinking and reasoning in one trace, MRP makes the meta-thinking explicit but still updates one LM end-to-end.
  • Middle is single-turn ReMA with separately parameterized high-level and low-level agents; alternating freeze/update keeps each gradient on-policy with respect to its partner.
  • Right is the multi-turn Multi-Agent Meta-thinking Reasoning Process (MAMRP) extension. Both agents share parameters and are distinguished only by system prompts, and stability over long rollouts comes from a turn-level PPO ratio that averages token-level ratios within a turn before clipping, instead of clipping each token independently:

Results

Motivating experiment

Setup:

  • Base model: Qwen2.5-Math-7B.
  • Three single-agent training schemes:
    1. RL from the base model directly on MATH.
    2. RL after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on GPT-4o’s step-by-step answers.
    3. RL after SFT on GPT-4o’s meta-thinking plans (single-agent MRP, not yet the multi-agent ReMA).
  • Benchmarks: MATH500 (in-distribution), GSM8K (easier in-distribution), AIME24 (out-of-distribution).

Findings:

  • On MATH500 and GSM8K, the SFT-warmed model wins — unsurprising, since it’s been shown the solution format.
  • On AIME24, the SFT baseline collapses, RL from base plateaus, and RL under meta-thinking keeps climbing.

That gap is the argument for decoupling meta-thinking from execution in the first place.

Main result

Setup:

  • Base models: Llama3-8B-Instruct, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
  • Baselines compared against ReMA: VRP (basic CoT), VRPRL (vanilla RL), and MRPRL (single-agent meta-thinking RL).
  • Math benchmarks: in-distribution (MATH500, GSM8K) and out-of-distribution (AIME24, AMC23, Gaokao2023en, Minerva Math, Olympiad Bench).
  • LLM-as-a-Judge benchmarks: RewardBench970, JudgeBench.
  • Each cell reports accuracy plus the improvement or degradation against basic CoT (VRP).

Findings:

  • ReMA wins four of five averages.
  • Largest gains on out-of-distribution math (AMC23, AIME24) and on the Llama3.1-8B Judge benchmarks.
  • The Qwen2.5-7B Judge average is the one case where single-agent MRP edges ReMA.

Other key findings

  • Multi-turn MAMRP converges and generalizes. During training, accuracy rises from ~55% to ~70%, and the multi-turn setup yields an average gain of ~5% across the seven test benchmarks.
  • Multi-turn is hyperparameter-sensitive. Some configurations trigger an “Echo Trap” — massive intra-turn repetitions or empty turns after a few rollouts — attributed to long-horizon credit assignment.
  • Turn-level ratio improves sample efficiency. Trajectory-level loss with the turn-averaged ratio reaches higher training rewards with fewer steps than the token-level variant; parameter sharing with simultaneous updates also converges noticeably faster than separate-weight settings.
  • Capacity gates format-aware meta-thinking. With structured JSON actions, smaller LMs collapse to the simplest “EMPTY” action to dodge formatting penalties, while 8B-scale models adapt their meta-thinking strategy to problem difficulty.
  • Generalization tracks the meta-thinking split. ReMA’s lead is largest on harder out-of-distribution problems like AIME24, consistent with the high-level agent surfacing strategic structure that single-agent baselines miss.

My Notes

  • The split-agent pattern keeps showing up across very different setups. A year later, a training-free engineering-design paper, Supervising Ralph Wiggum [6], runs a prompted version of the same architecture (one design agent plus a second agent that critiques its metacognition) and gets the same direction of result on a battery-pack optimization task. Adaptive Collaboration with Humans (HILA) [7] replaces the meta-thinker with a metacognitive routing policy that gates between autonomous solving and human deferral, again as a separately optimized layer. The Metacognitive Harness [8] wires Nelson–Narens feeling-of-knowing and judgment-of-learning signals into a test-time control loop, separating the monitoring layer from the reasoning layer at inference. Cog-Rethinker [9] inserts a metacognitive two-stage rollout on top of zero-RL so weak base models stop spending samples on problems they can’t solve. Different decouplings — separately parameterized vs. prompt-distinguished, training vs. test-time, math vs. engineering vs. human-in-the-loop — but the underlying observation is consistent: when reasoning is hard, putting the meta-level work in its own loop tends to outperform asking one model to do both.

  • The R1 comparison needs compute parity. ReMA’s headline is that decoupling beats mixing on the same training data, but two models updated with MARL is not the same training budget as one model updated with single-agent RL. A matched-FLOPs comparison against the best available R1-style baseline would decide whether decoupling is a real architectural win or just more effective capacity in a different shape.

  • Parameter sharing in the multi-turn setup blurs the two-agent story. The multi-turn extension has both agents share identical model weights, with their roles defined by differing system prompts rather than by parameterization. That’s a practical efficiency choice, but it narrows the architectural gap between ReMA’s “two separately parameterized models” and a single-model role-conditioned baseline. If the multi-turn results hold at scale, the decoupling claim becomes more about aligned RL objectives than about model capacity.

  • The multi-turn extension is the result that matters most for agent applications. Single-turn math is a clean benchmark but a poor proxy for how agents actually run. Real deployment means long rollouts and sparse rewards. The paper’s multi-turn extension (turn-level ratio plus parameter sharing) is where the architecture would actually be exercised in production, and the reported training curves are early evidence. Scaling to longer horizons and richer environments is the experiment that would decide whether this is a math-benchmark result or a default setup for reasoning agents.

  • Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Exploring a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design: the same split-agent pattern, training-free and on an engineering task, reaching the same direction of result.
  • Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning: another separately optimized metacognitive layer, here a routing policy that gates between autonomous solving and human deferral.
  • AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking: a related RL-on-reasoning recipe that, like ReMA, rewards a meta-level abstraction step distinct from the answer itself.
  • LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling: a test-time version of separating the monitoring layer from the reasoning layer, which ReMA does at training time.

item.title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies (ICLR 2026) [1], Han Zhou et al. (Google, University of Cambridge) introduce MASS, a multi-stage search framework that interleaves prompt optimization and topology optimization to discover effective multi-agent system designs.

Large language models, employed as multiple agents that interact and collaborate with each other, have excelled at solving complex tasks. The agents are programmed with prompts that declare their functionality, along with the topologies that orchestrate interactions across agents. Designing prompts and topologies for multi-agent systems (MAS) is inherently complex. To automate the entire design process, we first conduct an in-depth analysis of the design space aiming to understand the factors behind building effective MAS. We reveal that prompts together with topologies play critical roles in enabling more effective MAS design. Based on the insights, we propose Multi-Agent System Search (MASS), a MAS optimization framework that efficiently exploits the complex MAS design space by interleaving its optimization stages, from local to global, from prompts to topologies, over three stages: 1) block-level (local) prompt optimization; 2) workflow topology optimization; 3) workflow-level (global) prompt optimization, where each stage is conditioned on the iteratively optimized prompts/topologies from former stages. We show that MASS-optimized multi-agent systems outperform a spectrum of existing alternatives by a substantial margin. Based on the MASS-found systems, we finally propose design principles behind building effective multi-agent systems.

Methods

MASS is a three-stage search, local-to-global and prompts-to-topology-to-prompts. Stage 1 runs block-level prompt optimization (MIPRO from DSPy [5]) on each candidate building block individually and keeps the best-performing one. A block here is the paper’s term for a small pattern of agents collaborating on one function. The paper enumerates five: Aggregate (e.g., self-consistency), Reflect (e.g., self-refine), Debate, Summarize, and Tool-use. Stage 2 samples from an influence-weighted design space of topologies, fusing in Stage 1’s optimized prompts at each candidate. The paper prunes the topology search space so rejection sampling doesn’t waste compute on topologies unlikely to help. Stage 3 runs MIPRO again, this time over the winning topology’s full workflow-level prompt set. Each stage is conditioned on the iteratively optimized prompts and topologies from the prior stages.

Results

MASS is evaluated on eight benchmarks spanning reasoning (MATH), multi-hop QA (DROP, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMQA), and coding (MBPP, HumanEval, and LiveCodeBench’s test-output-prediction subtask). On Gemini 1.5 Pro, MASS averages 78.79 across the eight tasks, well above multi-agent debate (70.26), ADAS (69.72), and single-agent CoT (65.28). The Gemini 1.5 Flash ordering is the same; the table below has the full numbers. Figure 5 decomposes the Gemini 1.5 Pro gain into its three stages: block-level prompt optimization contributes roughly 6%, topology search another 3%, and workflow-level prompt optimization a final 2%.

Average across the 8 evaluation tasks (accuracy for MATH and LiveCodeBench, F1 for DROP / HotpotQA / MuSiQue / 2WikiMQA, pass@1 for MBPP / HumanEval). Table 1 from the paper [1].
Method Gemini 1.5 Pro Avg. Gemini 1.5 Flash Avg.
CoT 65.28 60.87
Self-Consistency 68.18 63.50
Self-Refine 66.90 63.46
Multi-Agent Debate 70.26 65.91
ADAS 69.72 64.75
MASS 78.79 74.30

My Notes

  • Topology gets quietly demoted. The paper’s stage-wise ablation shows roughly 6% gain from block-level prompt optimization, 3% from topology search, and 2% from workflow-level prompt optimization on Gemini 1.5 Pro. Prompts at both ends of the pipeline dominate, and topology contributes the least. That contradicts the implicit thesis of the topology-first generation (ADAS [2], AFlow [3]), which spent its complexity budget on what the agents look like rather than how they’re individually instructed. The paper’s own related-work section acknowledges this: “the importance of prompt designs has been relatively under-studied in these prior works.” It’s a stronger claim than the paper presents it as.

  • MASS layers a staged search around MIPRO. Stage 1 and Stage 3 both run MIPRO [4], the prompt-optimizer from the DSPy [5] ecosystem. Stage 2 does rejection sampling over a pruned topology space. MASS’s contribution is the staging discipline and the search-space pruning. The prompt-optimization workhorse is plug-and-play, and MIPRO is what MASS happens to use. MetaSPO [6] works the same way: the staging (bilevel meta-learning) is the contribution, and the prompt-optimization primitive it builds on (textual gradients) is off-the-shelf. EvoPrompt [7] inverts it: the primitive is the contribution (using an LLM to implement crossover and mutation), while the staging is borrowed from classical evolutionary algorithms. All three combine an LLM-as-optimizer primitive with a staging wrapper, but they differ in which piece is novel: MASS and MetaSPO add staging on top of a known optimizer, while EvoPrompt swaps the primitive into a known staging scheme.

  • AFlow’s competitive showing deserves attention. AFlow has no explicit prompt-optimization stage but stays close to MASS on 2WikiMQA and HumanEval. The paper attributes this to AFlow’s “expansion” phase, which uses error-log gradients à la Pryzant et al.: implicit prompt updating disguised as topology search. Where MASS pulls ahead most (MATH, MuSiQue) is where that error-log signal is weak. One-pass error-driven updates don’t make up for the lack of a dedicated optimization phase. The follow-up worth running: an explicit Stage 1 prompt opt fed into AFlow’s MCTS, to test whether the staging or the optimizer choice is doing the work.

  • Generalization beyond the eight benchmarks is open. Tasks span MATH, DROP, HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue, HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench, all static evaluation sets. The MASS-discovered topologies (debate-then-aggregate on MATH; summarize-then-execute on coding) are presented as design principles, but whether a topology learned on MATH transfers to RAG, agentic web tasks, or interactive embodied tasks is untested. This is also where the MAST taxonomy of multi-agent failures gets relevant: design-side optimization assumes the failure modes you’ll hit at deployment look like the ones you optimized against.

References

item.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines [1] (ICLR 2024), Omar Khattab et al. (Stanford and collaborators) introduce a programming model that treats LM pipelines as composable, typed modules and compiles them via teleprompters that bootstrap their own few-shot demonstrations from a small unlabeled training set.

The ML community is rapidly exploring techniques for prompting language models (LMs) and for stacking them into pipelines that solve complex tasks. Unfortunately, existing LM pipelines are typically implemented using hard-coded “prompt templates”, i.e. lengthy strings discovered via trial and error. Toward a more systematic approach for developing and optimizing LM pipelines, we introduce DSPy, a programming model that abstracts LM pipelines as text transformation graphs, or imperative computational graphs where LMs are invoked through declarative modules. DSPy modules are parameterized, meaning they can learn how to apply compositions of prompting, finetuning, augmentation, and reasoning techniques. We design a compiler that will optimize any DSPy pipeline to maximize a given metric, by creating and collecting demonstrations. We conduct two case studies, showing that succinct DSPy programs can express and optimize pipelines that reason about math word problems, tackle multi-hop retrieval, answer complex questions, and control agent loops. Within minutes of compiling, DSPy can automatically produce pipelines that outperform out-of-the-box few-shot prompting as well as expert-created demonstrations for GPT-3.5 and Llama2-13b-chat. On top of that, DSPy programs compiled for relatively small LMs like 770M parameter T5 and Llama2-13b-chat are competitive with many approaches that rely on large and proprietary LMs like GPT-3.5 and on expert-written prompt chains. DSPy is available at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy.

Methods

The programming model rests on three abstractions. Signatures declare the input/output shape of an LM call as a natural-language type spec (e.g., "question -> answer" or "context, question -> rationale, answer"), which the framework expands into a prompt template. Modules implement signatures via specific techniques: Predict runs a single-shot LM call, ChainOfThought adds a rationale step, ReAct interleaves thought/action/observation for tool use. Modules can contain other modules, so a retrieval-augmented QA pipeline is just a Python class that composes Retrieve and ChainOfThought. Teleprompters are the compilers: given a program, a metric, and a small training set (inputs only, no intermediate labels), a teleprompter runs the program on the training examples with a “teacher” model, keeps traces where the final output satisfied the metric, and uses those traces as few-shot demonstrations in the compiled program. BootstrapFewShot is the default; variants add random search over candidate demonstrations, compose with a stronger teacher program, or finetune a smaller model on the bootstrapped traces. The human writes the program structure and the metric; the compiler figures out what to put inside each prompt.

Results

The paper runs two case studies: GSM8K grade-school math (200 train / 300 dev / 1.3k test) and HotPotQA multi-hop retrieval QA. Base models are GPT-3.5 and Llama2-13b-chat; one HotPotQA run uses 770M-parameter T5-Large as the compile target. On GSM8K, the same three-line ChainOfThought program goes from 25.2% test accuracy (vanilla GPT-3.5 with no compilation) to 81.6% with the bootstrap + ensemble teleprompter; Llama2-13b-chat reaches 46.9% with the ThoughtReflection program plus ensemble, versus 9.4% baseline. On HotPotQA, a simple multihop program with bootstrap raises GPT-3.5 test EM from 31.5% (fewshot baseline) to 39.6%, and the ensemble reaches 45.6% on half the test set. The 770M T5-Large compiled from a Llama2-13b-chat teacher hits 39.3% HotPotQA answer EM on the dev set, using only 200 labeled and 800 unlabeled questions. That’s roughly on par with the much larger base models.

My Notes

  • The programming model is the real contribution, and the teleprompters are interchangeable. Pre-DSPy prompt optimization worked at the string-template level. APE [2] and later EvoPrompt [3] searched over isolated prompt strings with LLM-implemented operators. DSPy moves optimization up a layer: because modules have typed signatures and compose into a graph, a teleprompter can treat any pipeline as a black box to optimize end-to-end against a single metric, bootstrapping intermediate demonstrations along the way. Putting composition at the module boundary is what enables pipeline-level search. MASS [4] can search over typed-module topologies because DSPy established the abstraction; its prompt optimization at block and workflow levels uses DSPy’s MIPRO teleprompter directly. The teleprompters themselves (bootstrap + random search) are conventional. The novelty is that they operate on a program rather than a prompt.

  • DSPy-styled distillation works: the 770M T5 result is the demonstration.

    • When DSPy compiles, the teacher model runs the program on training inputs; the metric filters complete-pipeline runs where the final output is correct; those good runs’ intermediate steps become demonstrations for the compiled program. No human annotates intermediate hops. Final-output supervision via the metric does that filtering.
    • Table 2 shows this in action: a 770M T5-Large, compiled from a Llama2-13b-chat teacher on 200 labeled + 800 unlabeled HotPotQA questions, reaches 39.3% answer EM on dev, within a few points of GPT-3.5 fewshot. The paper calls this “orders of magnitude lower costs for inference”; the stronger read is that for retrieval-heavy tasks with good pipeline structure, most of the capability lives in the pipeline, and the base model just has to execute the compiled prompts competently.
    • The distillation analogy is apt, with three caveats on what gets kept, what the student inherits, and what the procedure costs. Both let you train a smaller model without hand-labeled intermediate supervision; the teacher’s outputs stand in.
      • Distillation uses every teacher-generated input-output pair as student training data. DSPy uses only per-module steps from traces whose final pipeline output passed the metric; those steps become few-shot demonstrations inside each module’s prompt.
      • Distillation compiles the teacher’s capability into a single forward pass of the student; DSPy keeps the pipeline structure intact. The 770M T5 still runs the same multihop program, just with bootstrapped few-shot demos inside each module’s prompt.
      • Distillation trains the student via gradient descent over thousands to millions of teacher outputs on GPU clusters, taking days to weeks. DSPy’s default teleprompters do no gradient training; they just insert filtered demonstrations into the student program’s prompts. Even the finetune variant that produced the T5-770M result trains in minutes on 200 + 800 examples, with total compile cost bounded by a few hundred teacher inference calls.
    • Whether the pipeline gain stays significant as base models mature is an open question.

  • DSPy is a clean instance of extrinsic self-improvement. Humans design the programming model, pick the modules, write the metric, and choose the teleprompter strategy (bootstrap vs. random search vs. finetune). The LM only generates candidates that the compiler scores and keeps. The intrinsic metacognitive learning position paper [5] calls this out as the ceiling case: DSPy won’t decide that the task needs a different module type, or that the metric is misspecified, or that the teleprompter’s search strategy is a poor fit. Every one of those is wired in. In engineering or production settings that explicit control is often a feature. Teams need predictable, auditable behavior more than they need an agent that redesigns its own loop. The ceiling matters only when you measure against intrinsic.

  • DSPy has become a de facto substrate for both research and industrial LLM development.

    • Scale signals. 34K+ GitHub stars since January 2023. The dspy.ai “Community Use Cases” page lists 25+ named company deployments and 15+ published research papers built on DSPy, and is maintained as a growing index.
    • Research adoption runs beyond the cluster we’ve been reviewing: STORM (Wikipedia-article generation), Co-STORM, PATH (IR with 10 gold labels), IReRa (extreme classification with 10K+ labels), ECG-Chat (medical reports via GraphRAG), Palimpzest (declarative AI workload optimization), WangLab @ MEDIQA (Toronto’s competition winner), UMD’s suicide-detection system (beating 20-hour expert prompt engineering by 40%). Within this cluster, MASS uses DSPy’s MIPRO as its prompt-optimizer primitive and MetaSPO cites DSPy as prior art.
    • Industry adoption spans finance (Moody’s), healthcare (STChealth, Infinitus, Raia, Salomatic), legal (Truelaw), travel (JetBlue), semiconductor (Normal Computing), e-commerce (Sephora, Zoro UK), developer tooling (Replit), enterprise AI (Databricks, VMware, RadiantLogic), and security (Haize Labs red-teaming). The Databricks integration is particularly sticky: DSPy co-author Matei Zaharia is Databricks CTO, and DSPy now powers parts of their LM-judge, RAG, and agentic offerings.
    • Why the abstraction endured. Teleprompter algorithms keep evolving (MIPRO → MIPROv2 → GEPA, all listed on dspy.ai), but the programming model (signatures, modules, teleprompters) has stayed stable. New optimizers slot into the same surface.

References

T., Moazam, H., Miller, H., Zaharia, M., Potts, C. “DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024. https://openreview.net/forum?id=sY5N0zY5Od. arXiv preprint arXiv:2310.03714.

  3. Guo, Q., Wang, R., Guo, J., Li, B., Song, K., Tan, X., Liu, G., Bian, J., Yang, Y. “EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024. arXiv:2309.08532, September 15, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08532
  4. Zhou, H., Wan, X., Sun, R., Palangi, H., Iqbal, S., Vulić, I., Korhonen, A., Arık, S. Ö. “Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2502.02533), February 4, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02533

  • Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies: builds directly on DSPy, using its MIPRO teleprompter as the prompt-optimization primitive inside a topology search.
  • System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning: cites DSPy as prior art and extends the same line to a task-agnostic system prompt learned across tasks.
  • GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning: a later DSPy-ecosystem optimizer that slots into the same programming model, replacing bootstrap search with reflective rewrites.
  • Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: the position paper that classifies DSPy as the extrinsic-self-improvement ceiling case, where humans wire in every choice the compiler doesn’t make.

item.title: EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers [1] (ICLR 2024), Qingyan Guo et al. (Tsinghua University, Microsoft Research) propose using LLMs to implement the crossover and mutation operators of evolutionary algorithms over a population of discrete prompts, gradient-free.

Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in various tasks, but they rely on carefully crafted prompts that often demand substantial human effort. To automate this process, in this paper, we propose a novel framework for discrete prompt optimization, called EvoPrompt, which borrows the idea of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) as they exhibit good performance and fast convergence. To enable EAs to work on discrete prompts, which are natural language expressions that need to be coherent and human-readable, we connect LLMs with EAs. This approach allows us to simultaneously leverage the powerful language processing capabilities of LLMs and the efficient optimization performance of EAs. Specifically, abstaining from any gradients or parameters, EvoPrompt starts from a population of prompts and iteratively generates new prompts with LLMs based on the evolutionary operators, improving the population based on the development set. We optimize prompts for both closed- and open-source LLMs including GPT-3.5 and Alpaca, on 31 datasets covering language understanding, generation tasks, as well as BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) tasks. EvoPrompt significantly outperforms human-engineered prompts and existing methods for automatic prompt generation (e.g., up to 25% on BBH). Furthermore, EvoPrompt demonstrates that connecting LLMs with EAs creates synergies, which could inspire further research on the combination of LLMs and conventional algorithms.

Methods

The setup is an evolutionary search over natural-language prompts. Maintain a population of N prompts (N = 10 in most experiments), run for T iterations, and at each step: sample parent prompts, call an LLM to produce a child via an evolutionary operator, score the child on a held-out development set, and keep the top N. The non-standard piece is the operator. Instead of a token-level rewriting rule, the operator is itself an LLM prompt. The paper compares two variants. The genetic-algorithm (GA) variant asks the LLM to perform crossover and mutation on two parent prompts. The differential-evolution (DE) variant asks the LLM to identify the difference between two parents and apply that difference on top of a third base prompt, borrowing the structure of classical differential evolution.

Results

EvoPrompt is evaluated across 31 datasets: seven language-understanding classification tasks (SST-2, CR, MR, SST-5, AG’s News, TREC, Subj), one dialogue-summarization task (SAMSum), one simplification task (ASSET), and 23 Big-Bench Hard (BBH) reasoning tasks. Alpaca-7B is the base model for classification and generation; GPT-3.5 is the base for BBH. On the seven classification tasks (Alpaca-7B), EvoPrompt (DE) averages 77.05 accuracy versus APE’s (Zhou et al., 2022) 73.80. On the 23 BBH tasks (GPT-3.5), EvoPrompt (DE) averages 75.03 versus APE’s 71.85 and the no-optimization baseline’s 71.49. The peak per-task improvement on BBH is around 25%, visible in Figure 3 as the tallest bar at the right.

Average BBH accuracy across 23 tasks. Table 12 from the paper [1].
Method Avg. accuracy on 23 BBH tasks (GPT-3.5)
Baseline (manual) 71.49
APE (Zhou et al., 2022) 71.85
EvoPrompt (GA) 74.18
EvoPrompt (DE) 75.03

Beyond the main results, the paper ablates population size. Figure 6 sweeps population size from 4 to 12 on three datasets: SST-5 (five-way sentiment classification), Subj (subjectivity classification), and ASSET (simplification). The three curves have noticeably different shapes.

My Notes

  • One of the earliest clean instances of “LLM as optimization operator.” EvoPrompt (September 2023) is among the cleanest early examples of using an LLM not as the thing being optimized but as the operator that performs the optimization step. Token-level random mutation produces incoherent prompts; an LLM mutation operator preserves semantics. Pryzant et al.’s APO [2] (textual gradients, EMNLP 2023) makes a parallel move from the gradient-descent direction. The same pattern then shows up across the prompt-and-agent-design literature: MASS’s prompt + topology stages [3] and MetaSPO’s bilevel meta-learning loop [4] are LLM-as-optimizer with different staging.

  • Why DE vs GA matters for prompts specifically. The paper compares Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Differential Evolution (DE) variants, and DE wins on most BBH tasks. Both operators are implemented by the LLM, so the contrast is semantic rather than tokenwise: GA’s LLM-prompt asks for a child that inherits from two parents, while DE’s LLM-prompt asks the model to apply the difference between two parent prompts on top of a third base. DE’s “find what’s distinctive and graft it onto the current best” maps more cleanly onto prompt refinement than GA’s “combine bits of each.” Subsequent prompt-optimization papers tend to describe everything as “evolutionary” without specifying which operator.

  • DE’s advantage reverses on simple generation tasks. On ASSET (a sentence-simplification benchmark: rewrite a sentence more accessibly while preserving meaning, scored by SARI against human references), Figure 6 shows GA matching or edging out DE across several population sizes. The mechanism is consistent with the rest of the paper: DE’s “apply the difference” move pays off only when the population encodes meaningful task-specific variation. ASSET’s good-prompt space is narrow (the useful phrasings all look like “simplify this while preserving meaning”), so the differences between parents are small or noisy, and applying that noise on top of a base destabilizes a prompt that was already near-optimal. GA’s conservative interpolation stays inside the narrow good-prompt band. Practical takeaway: if the task has a narrow good-prompt manifold (simple generation, canonical phrasings), default to GA; DE is the better fit when prompt diversity carries real signal (hard classification, reasoning).

  • The 25% headline is a single-task peak; the average is closer to 3.5%. The “up to 25% on BBH” claim in the abstract is EvoPrompt (DE)’s best per-task improvement across 23 BBH tasks; the average gain over the baseline is closer to 3.5% (Table 12). BBH in this paper is run on GPT-3.5, not Alpaca-7B. Alpaca is used only for classification and generation tasks. That raises a question this paper does not answer: as base-model capability rises, do prompt-optimization gains shrink, and does this whole direction have diminishing returns at GPT-4-class capability?

  • Population size depends on task complexity. Figure 6 sweeps population sizes from 4 to 12 on SST-5, Subj, and ASSET. For the simple generation task (ASSET), population 6 matches population 10 at roughly 2.5× less compute; for the harder classification task (Subj), larger populations with more diversity keep helping. Most LLM-as-optimizer papers default to population sizes of 10 to 30 without an ablation. Practical takeaway: tune population to task complexity rather than defaulting upward.

  • All of this is extrinsic by Liu and van der Schaar’s definition. The position paper on intrinsic metacognitive learning [5] argues that today’s “self-improving” pipelines rely on hand-designed loops: the search algorithm, what to optimize, against what objective, in what order, all wired in by the system designer. EvoPrompt is a clean instance. Humans pick the population structure, the GA-vs-DE operator, the development-set scoring, the termination criterion. The agent only generates candidates; it doesn’t choose what’s being optimized. None of this makes the result wrong, but it bounds the long-term claim: whatever the strongest extrinsic prompt-optimizer turns out to be, the position-paper bet is that an architecture which lets the agent decide how to optimize itself will eventually overtake it.

item.title: SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution? (ICLR 2026) [1], Michael Kirchhof et al. at Apple and the Tübingen AI Center introduce an information-theoretic metric for evaluating whether a single text summary a large language model (LLM) writes about its own uncertainty actually matches the distribution of answers the same model would produce if sampled many times.

The common approach to communicate a large language model’s (LLM) uncertainty is to add a percentage number or a hedging word to its response. But is this all we can do? Instead of generating a single answer and then hedging it, an LLM that is fully transparent to the user needs to be able to reflect on its internal belief distribution and output a summary of all options it deems possible, and how likely they are. To test whether LLMs possess this capability, we develop the SelfReflect metric, an information-theoretic distance between a given summary and a distribution over answers. In interventional and human studies, we find that SelfReflect indicates even slight deviations, yielding a fine measure of faithfulness between a summary string and an LLM’s actual internal distribution over answers. With SelfReflect, we make a resounding negative observation: modern LLMs are, across the board, incapable of revealing what they are uncertain about, neither through reasoning, nor chains-of-thoughts, nor explicit finetuning. However, we do find that LLMs are able to generate faithful summaries of their uncertainties if we help them by sampling multiple outputs and feeding them back into the context. This simple approach shines a light at the universal way of communicating LLM uncertainties whose future development the SelfReflect score enables. To support the development of this universal form of LLM uncertainties, we publish the code that implements our metric for arbitrary LLMs under https://github.com/apple/ml-selfreflect.

Methods

How the metric works. Input: a candidate summary string , a query , and sampling access to the model . Output: a scalar distance, lower meaning the summary is more faithful to the model’s answer distribution. The paper defines a good summary as one that is predictively sufficient of the answer distribution . Intuitively, if you’ve read , you shouldn’t gain much by also reading a fresh sample from the model. Operationally, the paper turns this into a Cloze-style test. Sample answers from the model for query , then take a separate sample and mask a word in it. Ask a judge LLM to predict the masked word twice: once given the candidate summary as context, once given the concatenated samples as context. Each prediction is a distribution over the vocabulary. The SelfReflect score is the 1-Wasserstein distance between those two distributions, averaged over many masked words and queries. A summary that truly captures the answer distribution produces the same predictions as the samples do; a summary that misses facts or misweights them shifts the predicted distribution.

Results

Across 20 modern LLMs tested with prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO), none produce summary strings that faithfully reflect their internal answer distribution. Summaries look right in form (they list possibilities and assign relative likelihoods), but the listed possibilities are not the ones the model actually samples. The fix that does work is mechanical: sample outputs from the model, feed them back as context, and ask the model to summarize those. The resulting summary is faithful.

In the benchmark’s interventional study (taking 3 × 1,000 open-ended questions and generating known-good, known-bad, and “almost-good” summaries with Gemini 2.0 Flash), SelfReflect cleanly separates near-misses where other metrics cannot:

Discriminating an almost-good summary from a good one is the setting that matters for “did the LLM really convey its uncertainty?”, and that is the column where the LM-judge baseline drops near chance (47.3%) and other traditional baselines do only modestly better.

My Notes

  • The negative result matters more than the metric. The literature on LLM self-reports has been accumulating evidence in one direction for a few years now: chain-of-thought explanations don’t necessarily reflect the actual computation [2], verbalized confidence is systematically overconfident across five widely-used LLMs [3], and now text self-summaries of internal answer distributions don’t match those distributions either. Each result is locally about a different self-report channel, but the pattern across them converges: when an LLM tells you something about itself, the right prior is that the statement is shaped by self-report patterns picked up from training data, not by introspection on the actual generative process. Liu and van der Schaar’s position paper on intrinsic metacognitive learning [5] argues that genuine self-improving agents need intrinsic metacognitive capabilities, with the ingredients at least partly present in current LLMs. SelfReflect’s negative result is a direct empirical bound on one facet of the metacognitive-knowledge ingredient: the ability to faithfully describe one’s own answer distribution.

  • The “sample-then-summarize” workaround is the practical bottom line and it has pipeline implications. The paper shows that LLMs can write faithful uncertainty summaries. They just need the samples in context first. That makes the missing capability not summary-writing but introspection on their own answer distribution without sampling it. For agent and product designers: if you want a calibrated multi-option response, use i.i.d. sampling plus a summarization pass. A clever prompt asking the model to “be honest about your uncertainty” won’t substitute for the samples. The cost is forward passes; the upside is a summary the SelfReflect metric scores as faithful.

  • The metric is more discriminating than the alternatives. Most evaluation work in this area has leaned on either LM-judge metrics (which have known failure modes) or coarse calibration scores (which discard structure). An information-theoretic distance between a string and a distribution (predictive sufficiency, scored against the empirical answer distribution) discriminates good from almost-good summaries where LM judges and embedding distances do not. Whether downstream work picks it up is the open question; if so, future “LLMs reveal their uncertainties” claims will need to clear a real bar rather than a vibes check.

  • Three deployment uses beyond benchmarking. The same score plugs into several runtime loops the paper doesn’t explore. As a training reward it targets the property SFT and DPO miss under naive objectives: optimize against the metric directly and you train for faithful self-summary rather than a proxy. As an ops-time ablation signal it answers “given my model and my query distribution, which prompting regime yields the most faithful uncertainty reports?”, narrower than the paper’s capability ranking and closer to production tuning. As a sampled monitoring signal it audits a cheaper production path (e.g., direct verbalized uncertainty) on a subset of traffic: large divergence on the sampled queries means the cheaper path has drifted, and the operator should fall back to sample-then-summarize or route to human review. Per-query routing is not a sensible use because computing SelfReflect for a query already costs the samples that sample-then-summarize would need anyway.

  • Part of a broader push to ascertain a model’s epistemic status. Whether an LLM knows a fact, and whether it can accurately describe its own uncertainty, are both aspects of what the model actually knows versus what it claims. KGLens [4] targets factual knowledge by turning a knowledge graph into natural-language questions and comparing model answers to the graph’s facts. SelfReflect targets self-knowledge of uncertainty by comparing a written summary to the distribution the model actually samples. Both route around the problem that LLMs produce fluent output regardless of whether they know the answer, by grounding the measurement in a signal the model can’t game by sounding confident.

  3. Xiong, Miao, Zhiyuan Hu, Xinyang Lu, Yifei Li, Jie Fu, Junxian He, and Bryan Hooi. “Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024. arXiv:2306.13063, June 22, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13063
  4.
